S01: Welcome. Today we will explore **visual tools** that help people plan, understand and check their learning. Our main question is simple: how can AI support **independent thinking**?
S02: I am Marco Cremaschi, an assistant professor at the University of Milano-Bicocca. My work connects **AI**, knowledge and practical applications. Today I will focus on choices that **students and teachers** can make.
S44: **Whattadata** is a spin-off of the University of Milano-Bicocca. We work on data analysis, responsible AI and practical solutions. This experience connects research with the needs of **people using technology**.
S49: For our **MRU meeting**, we will follow a simple learning path: set a goal, make ideas visible and check them. Prepared examples let everyone join, including people without a personal **AI account**.
S48: The **EDU Forum workshop** connects these ideas with classroom practice. We will look at planning, feedback and self-assessment. We will also discuss **teacher judgement**, privacy and the risk of trusting an answer too quickly.
S50: For the **teacher workshop**, the aim is a reusable activity for your own subject. We will connect goals, visual representations and checks of understanding. You can work with the **prepared materials** or use your own tools.
S50QR: You can scan this **QR code** to open the presentation and materials. I will give you a moment. Keep the page available so you can return to the examples during the **activities**.
S50LEGEND: The icons show the **audience** for each slide. Some slides focus on teaching decisions; others are useful for both students and teachers. They help you see how each example connects with **your role**.
S51: Meet **Andrea**, our fictional student. He can program, but he still confuses some ideas about generative AI. We will follow his **learning process**. You do not need programming knowledge to follow the method.
S52: Andrea has four connected tasks: **read, represent, create and explain**. A working application is one result. His explanation, prediction and correction give us further **evidence of understanding**.
S52SDL: In **self-directed learning**, the learner takes an active role. Andrea identifies a need, chooses resources and checks his progress. Teachers and peers can help, while he remains responsible for his **learning choices**.
S52SA: **Self-assessment** starts with clear criteria. Andrea compares what he can explain with those criteria, identifies a gap and chooses a next step. The useful result is a **decision about improvement**.
S52EKESTIN: This **physics experiment** found better immediate results with a purpose-built AI tutor. The tutor used guidance and feedback, rather than simply giving answers. The result concerns this particular design and **immediate tests**, so we should be careful about wider claims.
S52EDENG: This review found an overall **positive pattern** for ChatGPT-supported activities. However, the studies used very different tasks and tests. Their results do not settle the question of **lasting understanding** for every learner or subject.
S52E: In this mathematics study, one group's practice scores were **48% higher** than the control group's. Later, without AI, their scores were **17% lower**. This is why we need to check what learners can do independently.
S53: This is Andrea's **assigned chapter**. The book was created for this workshop, with accurate explanations and real technical references. It gives every demonstration the same **source**, so we can compare outputs with the original text.
S53TOOLCHATGPT: We start with **ChatGPT**. We will explore ways to turn the same chapter into explanations, questions and practice. Keep Andrea's **learning goal** in mind while we look at the tools.
S53GPT: ChatGPT can help prepare **learning materials** in several formats. The important choice is what Andrea needs to do next. A useful response should lead to his own **explanation, practice or revision**.
S53SHORTCUTS: Let us distinguish **formal actions** from **informal shortcuts**. This will help us understand which behaviour comes from the interface and which behaviour we are asking for in a prompt.
S53TYPES: A **formal action** is offered by the application. An informal label, such as slash flashcard, is part of our **request**. We still need to describe the task, source and format; the label alone does not guarantee an interactive result.
S53FORMALWEB: Here I selected **Study** in the interface and supplied the chapter. ChatGPT asks one question and waits. Before reading its explanation, Andrea must decide whether a new definition changes **parameters or context**.
S53FORMALREADALOUD: **Read aloud** offers another way to access a response. This silent recording shows the menu and playback controls. Listening can support access, but Andrea still needs to **explain the idea** in his own words.
S53SHORTCUTCLOUD: Think of this cloud as a **menu of possibilities**. The review covered 79 labels: 30 produced interactive outputs and 49 produced static results. We will look at what each result actually supports, rather than memorising the **labels**.
S53CMD1: This group supports **recall and self-assessment**. Andrea can reveal answers, record difficulties and track progress. The important action happens before the reveal: he should first try to **retrieve the idea from memory**.
S53CMD2: These examples use **questions and feedback**. Some check a selected answer; others let the learner compare an explanation with a marking guide. We should distinguish **automatic checking** from points the learner assigns.
S53CMD3: These **games and exercises** offer different ways to practise the same concepts. Matching or choosing an answer is a starting point. I would also ask Andrea to **explain why** his choice makes sense.
S53CMD4: This final group supports **guided activities** and classroom tasks. Progress indicators can make the next action clear. To judge learning, we also need to read the **answers and explanations** behind the completed boxes.
S53DETAILQUIZ: In this **quiz**, Andrea answers first and then reads the feedback. An incorrect choice gives him something specific to revise. I would ask him to explain the **reason for the correction**.
S53DETAILQUIZGAME: The **quiz game** makes practice feel like a short challenge. Watch the choice, feedback and next question. Our learning goal is to explain the concept, rather than simply finish the **game**.
S53DETAILMATCHINGGAME: Here Andrea matches **concepts and definitions**. After each pair, he should explain the connection in a sentence. This gives us more information than a **correct match** alone.
S53DETAILMEMORYGAME: This **memory game** asks Andrea to find matching concepts and definitions. Finding a pair also depends on remembering its position. Afterwards, I would ask him to explain the **meaning of the pair**.
S53DETAILJEOPARDY: Andrea chooses a clue, attempts an answer and reveals the explanation. He then assigns his own **points**. The score is **self-assessment**, so the comparison with the expected answer matters.
S53DETAILMILLIONAIRE: In this game, Andrea chooses an answer and **locks it in** before seeing feedback. The changing game level gives a clear sequence. The useful discussion concerns the **reasoning behind each answer**.
S53DETAILCROSSWORD: The **crossword** practises key terms from the chapter. Hints and checking help Andrea revise an attempt. Once the words are complete, he should explain how **training, inference and context** differ.
S53DETAILMINDMAP: A **mind map** can organise a topic into branches. In this test, the result was a **static response**, rather than an interactive map. Andrea can use it as a draft and check the connections himself.
S53DETAILFILLINTHEBLANKS: Andrea completes the **missing terms** and checks his answers. Notice how he can correct an initial mistake. I would then ask him to explain the **whole sentence**, including why the chosen term fits.
S53DETAILFLASHCARD: The key action is **recall before reveal**. Andrea attempts the question, turns the card and compares his answer. His rating should reflect what he remembered, rather than how familiar the **revealed answer** looks.
S53DETAILELI5: This label requests a **simple explanation** with familiar examples. The recorded result is text. Simple language helps when it preserves the important **conditions and distinctions** in the chapter.
S53DETAILSORTINGGAME: Here Andrea **classifies examples** as training or inference. The feedback helps him correct a choice. Ask what changes in each case: the model's **parameters** or the information used for the current response.
S53DETAILCONCEPTQUIZ: A **concept quiz** should test the meaning behind a term. Andrea reads the explanation after choosing an answer. A useful follow-up is: can he apply the same **distinction** to a different example?
S53DETAILSUMMARY: A **summary** gives a shorter view of the source. This example produced static text. Andrea should check the main ideas against the chapter and then try to explain them **without reading the summary**.
S53DETAILLANGUAGEDRILL: This exercise practises the terms **training, inference and context**. Andrea can use a hint, check an answer and revise it. He should also connect each term with a **concrete example**.
S53DETAILBLUEPRINT: A **blueprint** can outline the parts of a project or idea. Here the output is a static draft. Andrea still needs to check whether the proposed **structure** matches the task and the chapter.
S53DETAILMULTIPLECHOICE: **Multiple choice** makes an answer easy to record and check. The explanation is just as important as the score. Ask Andrea why the chosen option fits and why one **alternative** fails.
S53DETAILRECALL: This activity asks Andrea to **answer from memory** before opening the explanation. He can hide the answer and try again. The aim is an independent explanation, followed by a **source check**.
S53DETAILGAPFINDER: The **gap finder** presents claims that need correction. Andrea writes his reasoning and compares it with an expected explanation. This makes a **misconception** visible and gives him a clear revision task.
S53DETAILBLACKBOARD: This **board-style explanation** presents the ideas with checks to reveal. Andrea can inspect the different views and compare answers. I would ask him to explain one **relationship** before opening the relevant check.
S53DETAILWHITEBOARD: A **whiteboard-style request** can help arrange ideas. This test returned a static response, not an editable canvas. Andrea can use the draft to build a board and explain the **connections** himself.
S53DETAILSKETCHNOTE: A **sketchnote** combines short notes with visual cues. The test reported a static image; this slide preserves the recorded observation. Any visual cue still needs to keep the **meaning of the source**.
S53DETAILFLOWCHART: A **flowchart** makes steps and decisions explicit. Here the response is a static draft. Before drawing it, Andrea should check the order and explain what each **arrow** means.
S53DETAILINFOGRAPHIC: An **infographic** can bring key information into one visual. The recorded result was a static image. Its labels, examples and relationships still need a **check against the chapter**.
S53DETAILTIMELINE: A **timeline** places stages or events in order. This example returned static text. The useful check is whether the **sequence** is correct and whether it suggests a connection that the source does not support.
S53DETAILVENN: A **Venn comparison** asks which features are shared and which are different. This result is static text. Andrea should justify the **overlap**, rather than assume that similar words describe the same process.
S53DETAILANALOGY: An **analogy** connects a new idea with something familiar. Andrea should say where the comparison helps and where it stops. A helpful image must preserve the concept's **limits**.
S53DETAILCOMIC: A **comic** can turn an explanation into a short story. The test recorded a static image, rather than an interactive activity. The sequence still needs a **source check** so the story keeps the concept accurate.
S53DETAILFEYNMAN: Here the request is to explain an idea in **simple words**, notice a gap and revise the explanation. The recorded response is static guidance. Andrea's own explanation is the useful **evidence**.
S53DETAILGLOSSARY: A **glossary** collects terms and short definitions. This is a static reference. To use it actively, Andrea can cover a definition and give his own explanation and **example**.
S53DETAILORAL: The demo uses a **typed summary** of an oral answer. Andrea compares it with the expected explanation and moves through the questions. In discussion, I would ask him to expand the **reasoning** aloud.
S53DETAILSPACEDREPETITION: Andrea reveals a card and **rates his recall**. In this example, the review intervals are suggestions. A useful longer-term routine includes another attempt on a later day, using **checked questions**.
S53DETAILEXAM: This **practice exam** combines written answers, model answers and a marking guide. Andrea assigns his own points after comparing the criteria. The total is a **self-assessed score**, not an automatic judgement of his explanation.
S53DETAILSTUDYPLAN: The **study plan** breaks a goal into manageable activities. Andrea marks progress and moves between steps. I would ask what he can now **explain or do** after completing each activity.
S53DETAILCHECKLIST: A **checklist** makes tasks and progress visible. Andrea can complete an item, reconsider it or reset the list. We still need a short **check of understanding** behind each tick.
S53DETAILCONCEPTMAP: A **concept map** connects ideas with labelled relationships. The recorded output is a static response. Andrea can rebuild it using clear linking words, such as **uses**, changes or produces.
S53DETAILPOMODORO: Use this widget to move through **study activities** and check recall. The generated clock did not show a reliable countdown, so I would use a separate **timer** for the study session.
S53DETAILFISHBONE: A **fishbone diagram** organises possible causes of a problem. This test returned static text. The proposed causes are ideas to investigate; Andrea should look for **evidence** before accepting a connection.
S53DETAILICEBERG: The **iceberg** format separates visible effects from possible underlying patterns. The test reported a static image. It can help us ask questions, but a hidden cause still needs **evidence**.
S53DETAILPYRAMID: A **pyramid** arranges ideas into levels. Here the response is a static draft. Andrea should explain why one idea belongs above another and whether that **hierarchy** fits the source.
S53DETAILTREE: A **tree** can show a topic and its branches. This test produced static text. The important check is whether the parent and child ideas have a clear **relationship**, rather than just a tidy layout.
S53DETAILANATOMYDIAGRAM: This request breaks a **system into parts** and explains their roles. The output is static text. Andrea should then connect those parts and explain how they **work together**.
S53DETAILCYCLEDIAGRAM: A **cycle diagram** highlights repetition. In our chapter example, a selected token becomes part of the next context. Andrea should explain what changes and what stays **fixed** during ordinary inference.
S53DETAILEXPLODEDVIEW: An **exploded view** separates components so we can discuss their roles. Here the response is a static description. Andrea still needs to explain how the parts **connect** in the complete system.
S53DETAILHANDWRITTEN: This label requests a **handwritten style**. The test returned static text. Style can change the presentation, but we should judge the **clarity and accuracy** of the explanation first.
S53DETAILDECISIONMATRIX: This **decision matrix** compares training, inference and retrieval. Andrea changes the process view and answers checks. The useful question is what changes in each case and what the **evidence actually establishes**.
S53DETAILONEPAGER: A **one-page overview** can keep the main ideas together. This result is a static draft. Andrea should check the content, then use it as a starting point for an **independent explanation**.
S53DETAILLABELEDDIAGRAM: A **labelled diagram** names the parts and explains their roles. This test returned static text. Labels become useful when Andrea can also describe the **relationships between the parts**.
S53DETAILMNEMONIC: A **mnemonic** gives a short cue for remembering information. This example is static text. After using the cue, Andrea should give the full **meaning** so a memorable phrase does not replace understanding.
S53DETAILMEMORYPALACEIMAGE: This request links ideas with **imagined locations**. The test reported a static image. Andrea should check that each location has a clear connection with the **concept** he wants to remember.
S53DETAILMEMORYHOOKS: **Memory hooks** connect unfamiliar ideas with memorable associations. The response here is static text. Andrea should choose a connection that makes sense to him and test whether he can **recall the idea**.
S53DETAILMNEMONICART: This request turns a **memory cue** into a visual composition. The test reported a static image. A useful picture should help Andrea recover the **correct concept**, including its important limits.
S53DETAILVISUALVOCAB: **Visual vocabulary** pairs terms with visual associations. Here the result is a static response. Ask Andrea to explain the term without relying only on the picture, and to give his own **example**.
S53DETAILEMOJISUMMARY: An **emoji summary** offers quick visual reminders alongside short text. This is a static result. It can act as a cue, while the learner still needs a clear **explanation in words**.
S53DETAILPICTUREMNEMONICS: This request associates concepts with **memorable pictures**. The test reported a static image. Andrea should check the association and then use it to explain the concept **accurately**.
S53DETAILCHEATSHEET: A **quick reference sheet** collects essential terms and rules. The recorded output is static text. Andrea can check it against the chapter and then close it for an **independent attempt**.
S53DETAILDEEPDIVE: A **deep dive** explores a topic in more detail. This response is static text. Start with one clear question, and check that the extra detail helps Andrea meet his **learning goal**.
S53DETAILMISTAKELOG: The **mistake log** records misconceptions and written corrections. Andrea can mark an item understood or leave it for another review. The important record is **why the original claim was wrong**.
S53DETAILSTEPBYSTEP: A **step-by-step explanation** makes the sequence visible. This example returned static text. Andrea should pause between steps and explain the **link to the next step**, rather than simply follow the list.
S53DETAILTWINEXAMPLE: Two **related examples** can reveal an important distinction. The response here is static text. Andrea should identify what stays the same, what changes and how that affects the **explanation**.
S53DETAILWORKEDEXAMPLE: A **worked example** shows a solution and its intermediate steps. This result is static text. I would cover the next step and ask Andrea to **predict and justify** it before revealing the solution.
S53DETAILSOCRATICMODE: This label asks for **guided questions**. The test returned a written response, rather than a dedicated widget. For a dialogue, request one question at a time and leave space for **Andrea's answer**.
S53DETAILCOMMONWRONG: Here we look at **common incorrect answers** and why they fail. The output is static text. Andrea should explain the correction and then produce a **new example** that makes the distinction clear.
S53DETAILREALWORLD: A **real-world example** connects an abstract idea with an application. This result is static text. Ask Andrea which part of the example shows the concept and where the **comparison has limits**.
S53DETAILCONNECTIT: This request connects a new idea with **existing knowledge**. The response is static text. Andrea should explain the connection in his own words and check that it does not introduce a **misconception**.
S53DETAILLESSONPLAN: A **lesson-plan draft** can connect goals, activities and checks. This is a static response. The teacher reviews the sequence and decides what **evidence of learning** each activity should produce.
S53DETAILSOURCEANALYSIS: **Source analysis** asks us to inspect claims, evidence and limitations. This response is a starting point. We still need to open the source and check the **relevant passage** ourselves.
S53DETAILCASESTUDY: Andrea compares three **experiments**: training a model, changing a prompt and adding retrieved material. He writes his reasoning before revealing explanations. The key question is **what changes in each experiment**.
S53DETAILLEARNINGOBJECTIVES: **Learning objectives** should describe what a learner can explain or do. The recorded response is static text. Check that the suggested actions are clear and that we can collect **evidence** for them.
S53DETAILRUBRIC: A **rubric** describes criteria and levels of performance. This output is a static draft. The teacher should check whether its descriptions refer to **observable understanding** and fit the assignment.
S53DETAILBLOOMQUESTIONS: These questions invite different kinds of **thinking**, from recall to applying and judging ideas. The response is static text. Check what each question actually asks the learner to **demonstrate**.
S53DETAILQUESTIONBANK: The **question bank** gives Andrea several questions with answers to reveal. He writes a response, compares it and marks it reviewed. Completing the review should lead to a clear **next step**.
S53DETAILFLIPPEDCLASSROOM: This **flipped-classroom plan** separates preparation before class from application together. The output is a static draft. Decide what students should prepare and what **evidence** they should bring to the shared activity.
S53DETAILDIFFERENTIATE: This request adapts **support and difficulty** to a learning need. The response is static text. Keep the goal clear, discuss the actual barrier with the learner and review the **suggested adaptation**.
S53DETAILEXITTICKET: The **exit ticket** asks three short questions at the end of learning. Andrea writes all his answers before seeing the explanations. He then uses the comparison for **self-assessment** and decides what to revise.
S53DETAILPEERASSESSMENT: **Peer assessment** starts with shared criteria. In this demonstration, a fictional peer assigns points and writes specific feedback. The useful result is a clear **strength and next improvement**, supported by the work.
S53DETAILWORKSHEET: In this **worksheet**, Andrea writes an answer, reveals a model answer and compares the criteria. He assigns his own points. Watch how the **written explanation** and the running total serve different purposes.
S53DETAILLEARNINGSTATIONS: The **learning stations** separate training, inference and context into short activities. Andrea writes, compares and marks each station complete. Returning to an earlier answer helps him see what he should **revise**.
S53DETAILSLIDES: This request produced a **presentation file**, rather than an interactive chat widget. Before presenting it, review the sequence, examples and references. Andrea should be able to **explain every slide** himself.
S53EX3: Here we can follow the complete **flashcard activity**. The chapter is attached, the request is sent and Andrea uses the cards. Notice the order: **attempt, reveal, compare and review**.
S53WIDGETWORKSHEET: This example makes the learner's **written answer** visible before the model answer appears. We can compare the two explanations and discuss a revision. The learner's own **reasoning** should remain part of the record.
S53SKILLSSECTION: We now move from individual prompt labels to **Agent Skills**. These package a reusable method, so the next examples focus on the **workflow** as well as the final output.
S53SKILLS: A **skill** combines instructions with resources and sometimes code. A compatible agent loads the method and uses its available tools. This gives more structure to a task, while the output still needs **review**.
S53SKILLHOSTS: These examples were recorded in **ChatGPT Work mode**. Other compatible agents can also use skill packages, but their tools and setup may differ. Check the actual **product and environment** before planning an activity.
S53SKILLSTUDY: These four skills support different **study actions**: explaining, building a study kit, drawing a diagram and preparing cards. We use the same chapter each time. Choose the workflow that helps Andrea's **next learning step**.
S53SKILLLEARN: This skill begins with a **diagnostic question** and waits for Andrea. He must explain what changes when information is added to a prompt. The feedback comes after his **own attempt**.
S53SKILLLEARNING: This workflow creates a **study kit** and short later reviews. The original quiz used unreliable keyword grading, which could misjudge an explanation. Use the **reviewed self-assessment version** and compare answers with its criteria.
S53SKILLMERMAID: The skill produces an **editable diagram** of training, inference and retrieval. Andrea can change the diagram, but first he should check each **arrow** against the chapter and explain the relationship aloud.
S53SKILLFLASHCARDS: Here the output is an **importable text deck**, rather than an interactive app. Each question asks for recall and includes a chapter reference. Andrea should answer first and then check the **source-based answer**.
S53SKILLRESEARCH: These skills support **critical reading** and reference checking. One examines an explanation; the other checks the identity of cited papers. Both require us to return to the **original material**.
S53SKILLCRITICAL: Andrea's draft contains **three claims to challenge**. The skill helps identify the problems and point back to the chapter. We should check the generated **critique** as carefully as the original explanation.
S53SKILLCITATIONS: First we check the **identity, year and venue** of each reference. A correct record tells us which paper we have found. We then need to read its relevant passage to check whether it **supports the claim**.
S53TOOLSSECTION: We will now explore specific **study tools**. For each one, keep two questions in mind: what learning action does it support, and what **evidence** should the learner produce?
S58TOOLGOBLIN: **Goblin.tools** offers several ways to work with tasks and text. We will start with planning, then look at explanations and wording. Andrea remains responsible for choosing the **useful suggestions**.
S58COMPILER: Compiler turns an unstructured study goal into suggested **actions**. In this recording, it proposes four tasks. Andrea should check that they keep his **learning goal** and fit the time he has.
S58: Magic ToDo breaks a task into **smaller steps** that Andrea can edit. The useful level of detail depends on where he is stuck. A longer list helps only when it makes the **next action** clearer.
S58ESTIMATOR: Estimator suggests a **rough time window**. Andrea can use it as a starting point for planning. He should compare it with the time he actually needs and **adjust the plan**.
S58TASKMASTER: Taskmaster focuses attention on **one task**. The recording shows the timer starting and pausing. Time on task is one record; Andrea's explanation or completed work gives us different **evidence of learning**.
S58PROFESSOR: Professor provides an **explanation and example** of training versus inference. Andrea should compare it with the chapter, especially what happens to parameters. Any analogy also needs a clear **boundary**.
S58FORMALIZER: Formalizer changes the **wording** of a draft. Compare the original with the more professional version. Check that the meaning and Andrea's remaining **uncertainty** survive the rewrite.
S59: A useful plan names a **clear next action**. Reading one paragraph and writing a short example is easier to start than a broad goal such as understanding an architecture. Add detail where it removes a **real obstacle**.
S60: Andrea chooses four blocks: **read, ask, reconstruct and apply**. Each block ends with something he can inspect. Completed tasks show activity; the content of his explanations and products shows **what he understands**.
S60A: Take **five minutes** to work with this case. Andrea has twenty subtasks and cannot choose a starting point. Reduce the plan to **three actions**, add one understanding check and keep one decision for Andrea himself.
S61TOOLNOTEBOOK: Next is **NotebookLM**, where we organise study around selected sources. We will follow the chapter into questions, citations and different study formats. The central habit remains **checking the original passage**.
S61: First we upload the chapter and inspect the imported text. We then choose the **sources** available for a question. This keeps the task focused, while we still check the **generated explanation**.
S61RESEARCH: The search offers **new sources** that we can inspect before importing. Finding a result is the beginning of a review. Check its relevance and quality before using it as **evidence**.
S61DEEP: Deep Research produces a **sourced report** for a larger question. We should inspect the material behind its claims. This feature requires an **adult account**, so check access before using the workflow with a group.
S62: A **focused question** gives Andrea a manageable explanation to check. Here he asks why an answer can change without retraining. He should compare the answer and its **references** with the chapter.
S63: Let us open the **citation** and read the original passage. Does it support the exact claim? In this example, the words **ordinary inference** matter because they state the condition under which parameters remain fixed.
S64: Ask for **one concept at a time**, followed by a question for the learner. Andrea should try an explanation before moving on. If the first step is unclear, more detail may not solve that **specific difficulty**.
S64SETTINGS: The **Learning Guide** lets us set a conversation goal and response length. Choose settings that leave room for Andrea to answer. The guide should support his **own explanation and practice**.
S65: The desk analogy can help explain **available context**. We also need to state its limit: a model does not read like a person. Andrea should be able to explain the concept **without the metaphor**.
S66: We can expand the **Mind Map** to explore the chapter's main ideas. A branch helps us find a topic. Andrea still needs to explain the **relationship** and check whether the chapter supports it.
S67: Andrea chooses an answer before reading the **quiz feedback**. This question concerns a definition supplied in a conversation. After the explanation appears, he should revise his reasoning and check it against the **chapter**.
S67CARDS: With **flashcards**, the attempt should come before the reveal. Andrea then judges what he actually recalled. Recognising a familiar answer after seeing it gives different information from **remembering it independently**.
S67TOOLANKI: **Anki** offers a way to continue reviewing questions over time. Before moving cards into a review routine, check their answers and make sure each question has a clear **learning purpose**.
S67SPACED: Andrea can import the **checked cards** and rate his recall honestly. These are prepared examples; this account-based workflow was not executed here. The useful routine is to attempt, compare and **review again later**.
S67TOOLKNOWT: **Knowt** is another option for organising flashcards and study practice. We will keep the chapter and the learning question the same, so the focus stays on the **review method**.
S67KNOWT: Knowt offers study modes for a set of **checked questions**. An account and usage limits apply. This workflow is a prepared example, rather than a recorded execution; check access before planning the **class activity**.
S67NOTES: A **saved note** keeps a useful response and its citations together. Saving preserves the wording, including any mistake. Check the explanation before using it again or making it a **new source**.
S67REPORTS: A **study guide** can organise the chapter into a useful reference. Andrea should review the definitions, examples and numerical claims. The guide then becomes material for his own **questions and explanations**.
S67AUDIO: This recording is silent, but it shows the **Audio Overview** and playback controls. In a study session, pause the discussion and explain one **concept in your own words** before continuing.
S67VIDEO: The **Video Overview** turns a selected topic into a visual explanation. Watch how the ideas are presented, then compare the examples and claims with the chapter. A clear video still needs **verification**.
S67INFO: The **infographic** places concepts into a visual comparison. Check every label and relationship against the source. This generation feature requires an **adult account**, which matters when choosing activities for a group.
S67SLIDES: This recording shows **slide generation and presentation**. Revision controls were inspected, but an edited deck was not demonstrated. Revisions need another **content check**, because they ignore sources and use the deck quota.
S67TABLES: A **table** can compare what changes, what stays fixed and the supporting passage. Read the column headings first. A column of **common misconceptions** contains errors to reject, rather than definitions to learn.
S67SHARE: This demonstration **inspects the sharing options**. A link to a chat view does not automatically give someone access to the notebook. Check the intended audience and the actual **access settings** before sharing.
S70TOOLNAPKIN: **Napkin AI** turns text into visual proposals. We will start with an explanation that has already been checked, then choose a **visual structure** that preserves its meaning.
S70: Paste a **checked passage**, then request a visual for that particular idea. Before generating, decide which relationships should appear. The visual tool proposes a layout; we remain responsible for the **content**.
S71: Choose the visual that keeps the **process accurate**. Training must remain separate from ordinary inference, and token generation needs a repeating cycle. Review the **labels and arrows** before colours or icons.
S72: Follow the **generation cycle**: text becomes tokens, the fixed model calculates probabilities, and a token is selected. That token joins the context for the next step. Andrea should explain **why the cycle repeats**.
S72REBUILD: Now close the book and **reconstruct one relationship**. Then reopen the chapter, compare and correct it. The explanation of an arrow gives us useful evidence of what Andrea can **understand independently**.
S72TOOLDRAWIO: **draw.io** gives us a canvas for precise diagrams. Andrea chooses the boxes and labels the arrows. The learning action is to explain the **relationship** represented by each connection.
S72DRAWIO: Andrea builds the path from **prompt and context** to inference and the next token. Ask what each arrow means. New context changes the input, while ordinary inference keeps the learned **parameters fixed**.
S72TOOLEXCALIDRAW: **Excalidraw** lets us sketch a relationship with a simpler freehand style. A quick drawing is useful when it helps Andrea make an idea visible and **explain it clearly**.
S72EXCALIDRAW: Here the key arrow shows **retrieved passages entering context**. Retrieval does not itself retrain the model. Ask Andrea why an irrelevant passage can still lead to an **unreliable answer**.
S72TOOLMINDMEISTER: **MindMeister** is another option for a branching map. The choice of tool should follow the relationship Andrea wants to represent and the **access he has**.
S72MINDMEISTER: This is a **prepared alternative**, rather than a recorded tool test. Andrea can rebuild a branching map, compare it with the chapter and justify one correction. Check the account and **map limits** before use.
S81TEACHERTOOLS: We now move to **tools for teachers**. Our focus changes from helping Andrea complete an activity to designing the **evidence** that will show what he understands.
S82: Keep the **goal, task and criterion** connected. If the goal concerns relationships between concepts, collect an explanation or a justified diagram. Judge what the learner can explain alongside the **assisted product**.
S83TOOLMAGICSCHOOL: **MagicSchool** can help prepare teaching materials. We will use a rubric draft as an example. The teacher provides the goal and checks whether the output describes **observable learning**.
S83: Provide the **learning goals, assignment and constraints**, without personal learner data. Generate a rubric draft, then review it against the chapter. The teacher decides whether the **criteria** fit the evidence needed.
S84: A useful descriptor names something we can **observe**. Here we replace a broad judgement with a specific distinction between parameters and context. The **teacher-reviewed rubric** can be used separately from a paid platform feature.
S84A: The first criterion concerns **concepts and relationships**. Naming the terms is a beginning. Stronger evidence explains the connections, states their conditions and applies them to a **new example**.
S84B: The second criterion concerns **process explanation**. Look for clear links from input to tokens, probabilities and selection. A commented diagram or an oral explanation can make the same **sequence of reasoning** visible.
S84C: The third criterion concerns **application and checking**. Andrea predicts, changes one condition, compares the result and revises his explanation. A strong response also recognises **uncertainty** in a single generated outcome.
S85: What changes when we enter a new prompt during **ordinary inference**? Give learners a moment to choose. The expected answer is context, but ask for a **reason**, because the selected letter gives limited evidence.
S85B: These questions look at **connections**. A token does not always match a whole word. In the diagram, the selected token joins the context and the calculation repeats. Ask learners to explain that **repeating step**.
S85C: With the input and scores fixed, higher **temperature** makes probabilities less concentrated. It does not guarantee one particular sampled token. Also ask learners to explain why **likely text can still be false**, using a new example.
S86TOOLFORMATIVE: **Formative** gives the teacher a place to collect responses. We will connect the questions with the same learning goal and **criteria** we have just discussed.
S86: State the goal and explain when materials or AI may be used. Collect choices, explanations and drawings. The teacher reviews the open responses using the **shared rubric**, while the platform keeps the **responses together**.
S87: Choose the response format for the **evidence you need**. A reason can clarify a selected answer; a drawing can reveal a missing link. When access is a problem, agree an **equivalent response option**.
S88: These are **invented responses** for discussing judgement. One student has a working product but a misconception; another uses vocabulary without the full process. Compare each response **criterion by criterion** before giving an overall judgement.
S89: Useful **feedback** specifies the next action. One learner revisits parameters and context; another adds the missing selection step. A stronger explanation can move to a new example. Each response leads to another **learner attempt**.
S89A: Take **five minutes** to adapt this to your subject. Choose a goal, design a task and name an observable criterion. Then identify one access barrier and offer an **equivalent way to respond**.
S90ACCESSIBILITYSECTION: Our next focus is **accessibility**. We will consider ways to access a source and express an answer, while keeping the **learning goal** clear.
S90: Start with the **actual barrier** and discuss it with the learner. Reading, writing and organisation may need different supports. Needs vary, so choose and check the **usefulness of the support** rather than assume one tool fits everyone.
S91TOOLEDGE: **Microsoft Edge** offers another way to work with readable text. We will look at presentation and listening options, then keep a separate **check of understanding**.
S91: Open the supported chapter page, adjust the **reading preferences** and try Read aloud. Then pause at one paragraph and explain its main relationship. Easier access should lead to the learner's **own attempt**.
S92: Short **segments and a glossary** can make the next step clearer. Compare each adapted explanation with the original. Keep the important conditions, and choose the right **level of detail** with the learner.
S93TOOLDICTATION: **Dictation** gives another way to put an explanation into writing. The learner speaks, then reads and checks the text. The key habit is **review before submission**.
S93: Dictate an explanation, then **read it back**. Check technical terms, punctuation and words such as not, which can reverse the meaning. Availability depends on the device and language **settings**.
S94: Keep the **conceptual goal** the same while agreeing an appropriate response mode. Reviewed text, an oral explanation or a commented diagram may show the intended understanding. Apply the **same conceptual criteria** to the evidence collected.
S95: We can transfer this **learning path** to another subject. Start with a source and a goal, make initial ideas visible, use support and check it. Finish with an **independent explanation** of a new example.
S96: We now have several kinds of **evidence**: the learning process, an assisted product and an independent explanation. Looking at them together helps us decide what Andrea understands and what his **next step** should be.
S97: Use this table to choose a **function**, rather than collect applications. Free access can still involve an account, quotas or other limits. Check those conditions and offer a **prepared alternative** when needed.
S97STUDY: These tools support two different actions: **drawing relationships** and **reviewing questions over time**. Choose the action that fits the learning need. The chapter and the checking method can remain the same across tools.
S97P: A **paid upgrade** is useful only when its added function meets a real need. Compare it with the available alternative and check current terms. The **learning goal** should guide the choice.
